analysis.one_liner: Uses negotiated drug-maker rebates to give uninsured people discounted prescription prices, backed by a tax penalty on manufacturers that refuse.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee in July 2010 and never received a hearing, a vote, or any further action before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have created a federal program, run by the Department of Health and Human Services, for people who have no public or private drug coverage. The government would negotiate rebates from drug manufacturers — comparable on average to the rebates Medicaid gets — and pass those savings to pharmacies, which would sell drugs to enrolled residents at a discount. To make manufacturers take part, the bill would strip the federal tax deduction for advertising and marketing expenses from any drug company that refused to sign on. It died in committee without a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: People with no meaningful prescription drug coverage — the uninsured and underinsured who fall outside Medicaid, Medicare, and employer plans. They would buy outpatient drugs at prices discounted by negotiated manufacturer rebates, and could not be charged more before the discount than other customers pay. Retail pharmacies also gain guaranteed reimbursement and dispensing fees for serving them.

how_it_helps.text: It directs HHS to negotiate manufacturer rebates comparable, on average, to the rebates obtained under the Medicaid drug program.

Those rebates would be passed to retail pharmacies, which would then sell outpatient drugs to qualified residents at a discount — and could not charge them more before the discount than other customers pay.
To push manufacturers to participate, the bill denies a federal tax deduction for drug advertising and marketing expenses to any manufacturer that refuses to sign a rebate agreement.
It guarantees participating pharmacies prompt reimbursement and reasonable dispensing fees, and bars extra participation fees, to keep drugstores from bearing the program's cost.

analysis.who_pays: Prescription drug manufacturers, who would pay quarterly rebates on drugs sold to qualified residents or lose the tax deduction for their advertising and marketing spending. Taxpayers would fund administrative costs, initially covered by an advance from the Treasury before rebate collections flowed in.

drawbacks.text: Rebates were pegged to the average percentage obtained in Medicaid, so the discounts negotiated for people outside the program could be smaller than the deepest discounts; the bill does not guarantee any specific price level.

The bill would use the tax code to pressure drug makers — denying advertising and marketing expense deductions to any manufacturer that refuses to join — an enforcement tool critics of similar provisions have called coercive.

Participating pharmacies would have to front the discounts to customers and wait for reimbursement from federal or state administrators, creating cash-flow and administrative burdens for small drugstores.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit — lower drug prices for uninsured people who currently pay full retail — is real and directly targeted. The costs are modest and honest: manufacturers would keep a smaller share of revenue, the tax code would be used as leverage against non-participants, and pharmacies and taxpayers would front administrative work until rebates arrived. A fair objection is that the negotiated rebates were pegged to Medicaid's average, which might deliver smaller discounts than the "fairer pricing" framing suggests, and that rebating through pharmacies adds middleman complexity. On the whole, the public benefit outweighs those design concerns.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee in July 2010, and the committee never took it up before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Michael Michaud introduced the America Rx Act of 2010 on July 27, 2010, with two cosponsors.
The same day, the bill was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce — the only action ever taken on it.
The 111th Congress ended January 3, 2011, with the bill still sitting in committee; it never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Prescription drug manufacturers, who avoided a rebate obligation and the advertising tax penalty; uninsured consumers gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Drug manufacturers who kept charging full price

for.name: Rep. Michael Michaud
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and secured its referral to Energy and Commerce.

for.name: Reps. Chellie Pingree (D-ME) and Raúl Grijalva (D)

against.name: Pharmaceutical Research and Manufacturers of America (PhRMA)
against.what_they_did: The pharmaceutical industry broadly opposed government negotiation of drug rebates and tax penalties on non-participating manufacturers during this period; no industry opposition activity on this specific bill appears in the record.

sides.party_line_note: Only three House Democrats ever backed the bill, and no committee or floor votes were ever held, so no partisan split on the merits appears in the record.

industries.note: They would have to pay quarterly rebates on drugs sold to the uninsured at negotiated discounts, or forfeit the federal tax deduction for their advertising and marketing spending. Their refusal-to-deal leverage over uninsured buyers would be removed.

Pharmacies would administer the discounts and be guaranteed prompt reimbursement plus dispensing fees with no extra participation charges, gaining customers among people who currently cannot afford their prescriptions.
